title: Cryptographic User Content Offload/Obfuscation

labels.name: needs implementer interest
labels.description: Moving the issue forward requires implementers to express interest

body:
### What problem are you trying to solve?

Like it or not, LLMs are starting to change how web applications get designed, built, and distributed. LLM-driven web application development amplifies existing implementation risk.

Over the years, this community and related web communities have built out extensive security features to provide safer cross-origin access via CORS, provide defense-in-depth controls via Content-Security-Policy, and work around information leakage with Referrer-Policy.

Many of these controls reduce risk by building off the same assumption: that it's reasonable and tractible to achieve some level of trust in the code you distribute to clients, and to cordon off untrusted or semi-trusted code in its own origins. Not just code provenance, where you establish that the code is the code you expect, but also code semantics - that you trust that the code won't misbehave. https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/2206 started this discussion years ago, and I'd like to see if there's appetite to revisit this conversation and expand its scope.

I make no claim that any of this is necessarily feasible 😆

---

**Problem:** sensitive content is accessible to all javascript operating on the page.

Use cases:

1. A "high security" email client that renders content for the user
   * Requirements:
     * Must be able to render text from the server for the user to see
     * Should be able to transfer text from the server to the DOM without any javascript having access to the plaintext
     * Should not be able to programmatically operate on/read the rendered text
2. A "high security" chat application that provides bidirectional communication
   * Requirements:
     * Must be able to render text from another client (over WebRTC) or the server (over websockets or `fetch`) for the user to see
     * Must accept textual input from the user via an `input[type=text]` or `textarea` (or, theoretically, a `contenteditable`)
     * Should be able to transfer text from DOM to server (or peer client) without any javascript having access to the plaintext
     * Server should be able to set some sort of policy to govern which circumstances client javascript could potentially read plaintext values
       * If the `input` field sensitivity is governed by a DOM attribute, then presumably any active content on the page could just strip that attribute - or render a new `input` without the attribute
       * This probably requires an "all or nothing" policy that might torpedo the whole idea - either all the content the user could provide is opaque, or any of it could be intercepted
     * Somehow aggregate event inputs to reduce information leakage on keystrokes (probably breaks a million js libraries)

I use "high security" in quotes because the security of an application is by no means only governed by its client-side implementation, nor would this functionality be a panacea. Rather, being able to mask sensitive content from any first- or third-party javascript would provide another powerful tool to help us reduce risk and build better defense-in-depth from poorly implemented code (e.g. LLM slop).

This functionality could help provide stronger meaning for applications boasting end-to-end encryption - rather than just making the claims about code provenance, it would let those applications make claims that the client code can't know what content you're passing around, even if the client code is compromised.

There's bound to be some information leakage. The layout engine needs to know how much text there is, so it can figure out the bounding box. DOM provides lots of ways to interact with the layout engine. I don't see a way around that, and there might be some pretty clever ways to fully determine the content (e.g. by repeatedly resizing the container?). I'm not clear on what happens to text selection APIs. Solving for these use-cases would probably have far-reaching implications.

It's possible that a "secure inputs" concept is a complete non-starter. How can a user distinguish between a browser-provided text input and an emulated input (where it's just a `div` with enough event listeners and paint to make it look like you're typing into a box)? You can't just obscure all keyboard input, because then how would shortcut keys and navigation keys work? A bad solution might be one based on how qubes decorates windows with a color border that is unique and unpredictable to the applications themselves - have the browser provide an outline for the text input, and educate the user on what it means (wow, hard problem).

### What solutions exist today?

One obvious approach for the text-rendering problem is to isolate it in an `iframe`. I'm pretty wary of iframes. In a past life when I did more work in web application land, I saw Chrome aggressively clean up the `iframe` we were using to deliver content (no, not ads) inside a third-party webpage. That created a lot of user frustration and friction. That said, it's the biggest hammer available, and when it works it works.

If it were sufficient to show the user pre-rendered text, then you could imagine delivering an image containing that text from another origin. That's not very accessible, but it would preserve confidentiality concerns from first- and third-party code misbehaving.

There might be some hairbrained scheme involving WebGL and shader-based decryption, but doing text rendering entirely in-shader seems pretty rough. It also wouldn't play nice with accessibility features.

### How would you solve it?

One solution might be to have some `OpaqueString` value that serves as some sort of blob.

Another solution - the one that excites me - might involve some scheme where the client and server negotiate a key pair (or maybe the server just supplies one in a way that the browser can see it but the page cannot), and the renderer process gets the counterpart to the server's key. Now the server can send the client javascript data encrypted under that key pair, and the client javascript can hand it off to the renderer. Presumably by some new set of DOM APIs (`encryptedTextContent`?). There's a lot of complexity here, to be sure.

### Anything else?

_No response_
